name: Hogmany

attributes.attribute: Scottish festival on the last day of the year, also called Hagmany
known as the night of the candles or the night of the pelting

a sheep's breastbone on a stick offered to the household

sources: Campbell, John Grigorson. Witchcraft and Second Sight in the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. Detroit: Singing Tree Press, 1970, 230.
Carmichael, Alexander. Carmina Gadelica: Hymns and Incantations. Hudson, N.Y.: Lindisfarne Press, 1992, 76-78, 579.

text: Hogmany is a Scottish festival. People also call it Hagmany. It marks the last day of the year in Scotland. The day is sometimes called the night of the candles or the night of the pelting. People kept candles lit all night. They decorated houses with holly. Adults used holly branches to whip boys for their protection. Each drop of blood drawn assured a year of good health. A man in a cowhide bellowed through the streets. Men and boys followed, throwing snowballs and striking him to make a loud sound. The procession followed the sun's course three times around the village. It struck each house for good luck and demanded treats or money. It repeated a nonsense rhyme. Inside a home the party offered the caisein-uchd, a sheep's breastbone on a stick, to the household. The traditions root in protective rituals meant to keep people healthy through the new year. They may once have been used for divination.
